newsitem.title: USA: Dornan opponent claims victory in U.S. House race.
newsitem.headline: Dornan opponent claims victory in U.S. House race.

text.p: Eight days after the election, Democratic challenger Loretta Sanchez claimed victory on Wednesday over arch-conservative Republican Congressman Robert Dornan, one of President Bill Clinton's most strident critics.

Sanchez, a 36-year-old Hispanic businesswoman and political newcomer, declared herself the winner in the House race in southern California's 46th District after her lead grew to 929 votes with only a few thousand ballots uncounted.
Dornan, who made a brief unsuccessful bid for the 1996 Republican presidential nomination and was seeking his 10th term in Congress, would not concede.
"I will not concede to an inarticulate, flaky, non-qualified person," Dornan told reporters at his district office.

The former Air Force pilot, known as "B-1 Bob" for his fiery rhetoric and uncompromising support of the military, charged voter fraud, saying he suspected some non-citizens had cast ballots for Sanchez.
He said the alleged fraud may have resulted from an organized effort by the Democratic Party and others to register Hispanics to vote.
"I want to subpoena every single absentee ballot envelope and all the voter rolls," Dornan said.
Dornan said he would not ask for a recount, but called on the Republican Party to investigate the alleged fraud.

"I'll be seeing if my party has the intestinal fortitude to follow through and see if non-citizens voted in this election," he said. "Bob Dornan is not going to stand alone and take the heat on this if this seat has been stolen."
But Rosalyn Lever, Orange County's registrar of voters, said "there has been no evidence presented to me of any voter fraud in this election."
Sanchez denounced Dornan's allegations as "an insult to the people who followed the rules and became citizens," and her campaign manager, Wylie Aitken, called the charges "sad and pathetic."
The White House had thrown its support behind Sanchez's effort to oust the tough-talking congressman who once called Clinton "the Chicken Little of Little Rock" and accused him of being corrupt.
"It would be one more late return that would give many of us cause for great cheer, if true," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry.

Sanchez said voters in Orange County, a traditional Republican stronghold, had sent a message that they were tired of "divisiveness." She told cheering supporters: "We can send a woman to Congress. We can send a Latina to Congress. We can send a Democrat to Congress."

Sanchez, who trailed Dornan by a slim 200-vote margin on election night, was leading on Wednesday with 46,270 votes to Dornan's 45,341. Another 1,000 absentee ballots remained to be counted along with up to 3,000 provisional ballots, which require validation because they were cast by people who had changed their addresses or who claimed to have lost their absentee ballots.
After a week of anxious waiting, Sanchez campaign officials contended it would be mathematically impossible for Dornan to overcome his deficit.

Sanchez, who received a congratulatory phone call from Vice President Al Gore, was so confident that she planned to be in Washington later this week for the orientation of new House members, her aides said.

During his 18 years in Congress, Dornan gained a reputation for strong opposition to abortion, communism, gay rights and gun control. He turned off some voters with his quixotic presidential bid, a move he defended as an attempt to sharpen the attack on Clinton.
Dornan told reporters he would consider an offer to host a conservative talk show if he lost his seat.
Sanchez, a financial analyst who had never held elected office, campaigned as a moderate while painting Dornan as an extremist out of step with the needs of his largely working-class constituents.
